docs.title: 2.2 My Topics
docs.text:
(1) Area of Law Information Law

(2) Primary Choice Provisional title: Contextual Assessment in EU Hate Speech Moderation: Legal Requirements, Implementation, and Legitimacy Risks Research question: This dissertation will analyse whether EU law requires online platforms—and, if so, to what extent—to conduct a contextual assessment when moderating hate speech, and identify the legal sources of any such requirement. It will further explore how contextual assessment could be implemented in large-scale content moderation and evaluate the legitimacy risks that such implementation may generate.

(3) Secondary Choice Provisional title: Meaningful Human Involvement Beyond “Solely Automated” Decision-Making: Formal vs Substantive Standards and Regulatory Detection of Token Review Research question: This dissertation will examine what constitutes meaningful human involvement such that a decision cannot be regarded as solely automated, and consider whether the relevant standard should be assessed on a formal or substantive basis. It will also explore how organisations may design processes that merely appear to involve human review, and how regulators can detect, scrutinise, and challenge such practices effectively.

docs.title: 2. Bibliographies
docs.text:
Items in bibliographies take the same form as all other citations in OSCOLA, with three exceptions: (1) the author’s surname should precede his or her initial(s), with no comma separating them, but a comma after the final initial; (2) only initials should be used, and not forenames; and (3) the titles of unattributed works should be preceded by a double em-dash.

Works should be arranged in alphabetical order of author surname, with unattributed works being listed at the beginning of the bibliography in alphabetical order of first major word of the title.

Example: CITATION in a footnote: Elizabeth Fisher, Risk Regulation and Administrative Constitutionalism (Hart Publishing 2007). CITATION in a bibliography: Fisher E, Risk Regulation and Administrative Constitutionalism (Hart Publishing 2007)

docs.title: 2.1 Seminar 1
docs.text:
[Chunck 010101] Key words: copyright weaponization; noncopyright interests; market exclusivity; economic incentives; legal strategy Essay-ready point: Copyright weaponization occurs when copyright is invoked not to protect market exclusivity or economic incentives, but to advance noncopyright interests such as suppression, retaliation, reputation management, or privacy protection. Original Sentence: All these stories have one thing in common: they all involve copyright owners using copyright to advance noncopyright interests. This Article refers to these actions as ‘weaponizing copyright.’ Page: 196

[Chunck 010102] Key words: copyright weaponization; utilitarian copyright; incentives; dissemination; market exclusivity; public benefit Essay-ready point: The article contrasts weaponized copyright with copyright’s conventional justification: copyright protects authors’ market exclusivity so that economic incentives will encourage socially valuable creation. Original Sentence: Copyright grants authors exclusive rights in their works in order to encourage creation and dissemination of socially valuable works. Page: 195

[Chunck 010103] Key words: copyright weaponization; economic interest; licensing market; copyright purpose; misuse; non-economic claims Essay-ready point: A central critique is that weaponized copyright does not serve copyright’s traditional function because the claimant is often not trying to preserve a licensing market or recover economic loss. Original Sentence: In none of these stories are individuals asserting copyright to protect their market exclusivity or economic interests — the intended purposes of copyright. Page: 197

[Chunck 010104] Key words: copyright weaponization; silencing; erasure; retaliation; reputation; privacy Essay-ready point: Smith identifies five recurring noncopyright objectives: erasing facts, suppressing criticism, punishing perceived wrongdoing, protecting reputation or moral rights, and preserving privacy. Original Sentence: The article identifies “five common noncopyright objectives”: “to silence and erase facts, suppress criticism and speech, punish and retaliate, protect reputation and moral rights, and preserve privacy.” Page: 197

[Chunck 010105] Key words: copyright weaponization; bad faith; vulnerable parties; defensive copyright; power imbalance; nuance Essay-ready point: A nuanced argument in the article is that non-economic uses of copyright should not automatically be treated as bad faith, because copyright may sometimes be used defensively by vulnerable people. Original Sentence: The first is that not all weaponized or noncopyright uses of copyright are bad, and the second is that not all typical copyright uses are good. Page: 197

[Chunck 010106] Key words: copyright weaponization; power dynamics; aggressor; vulnerable parties; legal weapon; defensive use Essay-ready point: Smith frames copyright as a legal weapon whose moral significance depends partly on who uses it: it may further domination when used by the powerful, but provide protection when used by the vulnerable. Original Sentence: A weapon can be in the hand of an aggressor to cause harm… or it can be in the hand of the vulnerable to even the playing field. Page: 197

[Chunck 010107] Key words: copyright weaponization; retaliation; punishment; spite; property rights; copyright abuse Essay-ready point: When copyright is used primarily to punish or retaliate, it resembles a spite-based assertion of property rights rather than an attempt to protect creative incentives. Original Sentence: In each of these instances, copyright is weaponized to punish and retaliate. Page: 201

[Chunck 010108] Key words: copyright weaponization; DMCA strike; PewDiePie; racist speech; sexist speech; retaliation Essay-ready point: The Campo Santo and Alinity examples show copyright strikes being used not to prevent market substitution, but to punish racist or sexist speech by a popular online figure. Original Sentence: Neither asserted copyright against PewDiePie to protect the market exclusivity or economic interests in their works. Instead, the primary objective ... was to punish PewDiePie. Page: 203

[Chunck 010109] Key words: copyright weaponization; injunction; chilling effect; litigation delay; suppression; TD Bank Essay-ready point: Even unsuccessful copyright weaponization may cause real harm because litigation and injunctions can suppress speech or distribution for extended periods before the claim is resolved. Original Sentence: TD Bank was successful in using copyright to suppress the dissemination of an author’s book for years. Page: 204

[Chunck 010110] Key words: copyright weaponization; information control; erasure; public knowledge; concealment; historical record Essay-ready point: Another form of weaponization occurs when copyright owners seek not to exploit their works, but to prevent public access to embarrassing, damaging, or politically inconvenient information. Original Sentence: Copyright is also weaponized to erase facts and bury information. Page: 207

[Chunck 010111] Key words: copyright weaponization; investigative journalism; Harvey Weinstein; Ronan Farrow; silencing victims; public interest Essay-ready point: The attempted use of copyright against Ronan Farrow illustrates how copyright threats may be deployed to obstruct journalism and silence victims, rather than to vindicate any economic copyright interest. Original Sentence: The copyright threats ... were not based on a market or financial interest ... but were an attempt to silence Weinstein’s victims. Page: 200

[Chunck 010112] Key words: copyright weaponization; memory holes; historical record; truth; public discourse; censorship Essay-ready point: Smith, drawing on Goldman and Silbey, argues that copyright can create social “memory holes” by removing facts and ideas from public circulation, thereby distorting collective memory and the search for truth. Original Sentence: Asserting copyright to erase facts and bury information can create ‘memory holes’ in society. Page: 213–214

[Chunck 010113] Key words: copyright weaponization; reputation; moral rights; dignity; association; expressive control Essay-ready point: Copyright may also be weaponized to protect reputation, dignity, or moral objections, especially where authors object to their works being associated with political, racist, or controversial messages. Original Sentence: Copyright is also weaponized to protect reputation, moral rights, and other dignitary interests. Page: 219

[Chunck 010114] Key words: copyright weaponization; privacy; revenge porn; intimate images; personal autonomy; defensive copyright Essay-ready point: The article treats privacy-based copyright claims as especially difficult because they may protect legitimate personal interests, such as removing intimate images from the internet, even though they remain outside copyright’s economic rationale. Original Sentence: Copyright is also weaponized to preserve privacy. Women use copyright to remove intimate photographs of themselves from the Internet. Page: 223

[Chunck 010115] Key words: copyright weaponization; copyright reform; legal gaps; vulnerable parties; privacy law; balanced framework Essay-ready point: Smith’s conclusion is that reform cannot simply condemn all copyright weaponization, because doing so might suppress harmful abuses but also remove one of the few available tools for vulnerable people seeking privacy, dignity, or protection. Original Sentence: Reforms ... need to be concurrent with reforms that strengthen laws or fill gaps that individuals are currently weaponizing copyright to fill. Page: 265

docs.title: 2.2 Seminar 2
docs.text:
[Chunck 020201] Key words: online copyright; everyday internet use; streaming; downloading; hyperlinking Essay-ready point: A useful starting point is that EU copyright law reaches many ordinary internet activities, including streaming, downloading, and even hyperlinking, because online copying and online dissemination may both trigger exclusive rights. Original Sentence: Activities like streaming music and films, downloading an e-book or news article, or even posting a hyperlink may, and often do, have copyright significance. Page: 386

[Chunck 020202] Key words: reproduction right; communication to the public; dissemination; EU copyright; exclusive rights Essay-ready point: In EU copyright law, online use is mainly structured around two exclusive rights: reproduction for copying protected content, and communication to the public for online dissemination. Original Sentence: Copying of protected content ... is subject to the right of reproduction. Online dissemination of that content to the general internet public is subject to the right of communication to the public. Page: 386

[Chunck 020203] Key words: Article 3 InfoSoc; CJEU; legal uncertainty; communication to the public; EU harmonisation Essay-ready point: The right of communication to the public, harmonised in Article 3 of the InfoSoc Directive, is one of the most contested areas of EU copyright law because CJEU case law has produced complex and uncertain criteria. Original Sentence: The right is harmonized in Article 3 of Directive 2001/29/EC (InfoSoc Directive) and its interpretation is perhaps the most controversial aspect of EU copyright law. Page: 386

[Chunck 020204] Key words: WCT; WPPT; making available; international copyright; digital environment Essay-ready point: The EU right of communication to the public builds on international copyright instruments, especially the WIPO treaties, which adapted communication rights to digital and on-demand environments. Original Sentence: The WCT includes a general exclusive right of communication to the public in Article 8. Both the WCT and WPPT include ... an exclusive right of ‘making available.’ Page: 387

[Chunck 020205] Key words: making available; access; online communication; liability; on-demand services Essay-ready point: For online communication, liability may arise from making a work available to the public even if no member of the public actually accesses or receives the work. Original Sentence: The ‘making available’ prong ... does not require simultaneous reception of the work by the public and is independent of whether, where, and how often the work is accessed. Page: 387

[Chunck 020206] Key words: autonomous concept; EU law; consistent interpretation; InfoSoc Directive; Rental and Lending Directive Essay-ready point: Because “communication to the public” is treated as an autonomous concept of EU law, it should be interpreted consistently across relevant EU copyright instruments. Original Sentence: ‘Communication to the public’ is an autonomous concept of EU law. Page: 388

[Chunck 020207] Key words: cumulative conditions; act of communication; public; CJEU framework; Article 3 Essay-ready point: The CJEU’s framework requires two essential cumulative conditions: there must be an act of communication, and that act must be directed to a public. Original Sentence: The first two main conditions are essential and cumulative ... The first cumulative condition is the existence of an ‘act of communication’ ... The second cumulative condition is that the communication is made to the ‘public.’ Page: 388

[Chunck 020208] Key words: intervention; knowledge; deliberate act; access; protected work Essay-ready point: A communication normally requires a deliberate intervention by the user, meaning that the user knowingly facilitates access to the protected work. Original Sentence: The user intervenes ‘in full knowledge of the consequences of his action, to give his customers access to a protected work.’ Page: 389

[Chunck 020209] Key words: indispensable intervention; Filmspeler; Ziggo; access facilitation; broad liability Essay-ready point: In online cases, the Court has moved away from a strict requirement that the intervention be indispensable, allowing liability where the defendant’s role merely makes access significantly easier. Original Sentence: In these cases, the intervention does not need to be indispensable. It suffices that it is very important. Page: 389

[Chunck 020210] Key words: primary liability; broad interpretation; intervention; exclusive right; online platforms Essay-ready point: By treating important facilitation as an act of communication, the CJEU broadens the range of online conduct capable of triggering primary copyright liability. Original Sentence: It surely allows a broader range of acts to qualify as an intervention, thereby broadening the range of activities that may fall within the scope of the exclusive right and give rise to primary liability. Page: 390

[Chunck 020211] Key words: public; indeterminate audience; de minimis threshold; private communication; recipients Essay-ready point: The “public” requirement excludes purely private communications and requires an indeterminate, fairly large group of potential recipients. Original Sentence: The public is defined as an ‘indeterminate’ and ‘fairly large number’ of recipients as potential beneficiaries of the communication. Page: 391

[Chunck 020212] Key words: new public; hyperlinking; authorisation; right holder; Svensson Essay-ready point: Where the same technical means are used, a communication may still infringe if it reaches a “new public,” meaning a public not considered by the right holder when authorising the initial communication. Original Sentence: A work is communicated to a ‘new public’ ... a public not taken into account by the copyright holder when they authorized the initial communication. Page: 392

[Chunck 020213] Key words: Svensson; hyperlinking; freely accessible content; new public; authorisation Essay-ready point: In Svensson, the CJEU treated hyperlinking as an act of making available, but held that links to freely accessible authorised content do not require a new authorisation because they do not reach a new public. Original Sentence: The CJEU first considered that the provision of direct access to the works via a link from one website to another is an act of making available ... However, to trigger Article 3(1) InfoSoc Directive, the acts ‘must also be directed at a new public.’ Page: 392

[Chunck 020214] Key words: GS Media; knowledge presumption; profit-making; unauthorised content; hyperlinking Essay-ready point: After GS Media, the legality of linking to unauthorised content depends heavily on knowledge, with commercial linkers facing a presumption that they knew the linked content was unauthorised. Original Sentence: After GS Media, it is arguable that [profit-making nature] plays a decisive role to establish a presumption of knowledge ... in scenarios of hyperlinking to works available online without the consent of the rights holder. Page: 398

[Chunck 020215] Key words: safe harbours; value gap; press publishers; platform liability; copyright reform Essay-ready point: Quintais argues that reform should not expand communication-to-the-public liability through press-publisher rights or platform filtering obligations; instead, it should clarify the right while preserving hosting safe harbours and avoiding conflicts with fundamental rights. Original Sentence: The article argues for abandoning the legislative proposals for a new right for press publishers and the so-called value gap ... Instead, reform should focus on redefining the right of communication to the public and preserving safe harbors, especially for hosting providers. Page: 385

[Chunck 020301] Key words: server rule; server test; direct liability; hyperlinking; Perfect 10 Essay-ready point: In U.S. law, the server rule generally prevents hyperlinking from constituting direct copyright infringement unless the defendant stores and serves the copyrighted content. Original Sentence: In the U.S., a judge-made doctrine known as the ‘server test’ or ‘server rule’ governs the treatment of hyperlinks under the Copyright Act. Page: 177

[Chunck 020302] Key words: Perfect 10 v Amazon; Ninth Circuit; server rule; precedent; hyperlink liability Essay-ready point: The leading U.S. authority is Perfect 10 v. Amazon, where the Ninth Circuit adopted the server rule and influenced later courts’ treatment of hyperlinking. Original Sentence: The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit adopted the test in a 2007 case, Perfect 10 v. Amazon, and several U.S. courts since then have followed it. Page: 177

[Chunck 020303] Key words: hyperlinking; store and serve; server location; display right; distribution; in-line linking Essay-ready point: Under the server rule, the decisive question is not whether the user sees the work through the defendant’s website, but whether the defendant’s own server stores and transmits the work. Original Sentence: Under the ‘server rule,’ ‘the owner of a computer that does not store and serve ... electronic information to a user is not displaying [or distributing] that information, even if such owner in-line links to or frames the electronic information.’ Page: 177

[Chunck 020304] Key words: hyperlinking; simple linking; deep linking; framing; in-line linking; direct infringement Essay-ready point: The server rule applies broadly to simple links, deep links, framing, and in-line links, meaning that hyperlink providers usually avoid direct infringement liability if they do not host the content. Original Sentence: A defendant who provides a hyperlink of any kind (through simple linking, deep linking, framing, or in-line linking) cannot incur direct copyright liability unless that defendant also ‘store[s] and serve[s]’ the copyrighted material to which the link points. Page: 177

[Chunck 020305] Key words: hyperlinking; Google Image Search; thumbnails; full-size images; third-party servers; fair use Essay-ready point: In Perfect 10, Google’s stored thumbnail images raised direct infringement issues, but full-size images shown through links did not, because those images were stored on third-party servers. Original Sentence: There was a fundamental distinction between the presentation of Google’s ‘thumbnail’ image copies (which were actually stored on Google servers) and the presentation of the full-sized images, which were not stored on Google servers but were instead served up to users through ‘framed’ or ‘in-line’ links. Page: 177–178

[Chunck 020306] Key words: hyperlinking; HTML instructions; lines of text; display right; Ninth Circuit; technical formalism Essay-ready point: The Ninth Circuit’s reasoning rests on the view that a hyperlink merely provides HTML instructions and therefore is not equivalent to showing or displaying a copyrighted copy. Original Sentence: The Ninth Circuit contended that a link is, essentially ‘HTML instructions [constituting mere] lines of text,’ and that ‘[p]roviding these HTML instructions is not equivalent to showing a copy.’ Page: 178

[Chunck 020307] Key words: secondary liability; facilitation; direct infringement; contributory infringement; hyperlinking Essay-ready point: Because hyperlinking is generally excluded from direct infringement under the server rule, U.S. courts tend to treat links as facilitation of infringement rather than infringement itself. Original Sentence: U.S. courts instead characterize the provision of hyperlinks of any form as the facilitation of a user’s access to infringing works, which ‘raises only [secondary] liability issues.’ Page: 179

[Chunck 020308] Key words: hyperlinking; statutory breadth; device or process; transmission; public display; server rule critique Essay-ready point: Ginsburg and Budiardjo argue that the server rule narrows the Copyright Act despite statutory language that broadly covers transmission or communication by any device or process. Original Sentence: Despite the breadth and technological neutrality of those rights, the server rule effectively assumes that a hyperlink is not a ‘device or process’ that ‘transmit[s] or otherwise communicate[s] a performance or display of a work ... to the public.’ Page: 179

[Chunck 020309] Key words: hyperlinking; transmission process; clickable links; HTML code; browser retrieval; public display Essay-ready point: A strong critique of the server rule is that clickable hyperlinks do more than identify location: they initiate the technical process by which the user’s browser retrieves and displays the work. Original Sentence: The ‘process ... whereby images ... are received’ on a user’s screen certainly includes the hyperlinks and HTML code which cause that image to appear. Page: 179–180

[Chunck 020310] Key words: hyperlinking; misplaced metaphors; library index; driving directions; trigger function; clickable links Essay-ready point: The article criticises analogies that treat hyperlinks as mere library indexes or driving directions, because clickable links also trigger the delivery of content to the user. Original Sentence: Hyperlinks do provide information about the online location of the content that the user seeks to access. This locational-information function is, indeed, analogous to the function fulfilled by a ‘library’s card index’ or ‘driving directions’ ... However, most hyperlinks are clickable ... and therefore these hyperlinks also act as a trigger. Page: 183

[Chunck 020311] Key words: hyperlinking; deep links; in-line links; framing; direct access; contextual control Essay-ready point: Deep links and in-line links are more legally significant than simple references because they can deliver the content directly, bypass navigation, and frame the work within a new context. Original Sentence: Deep links and in-line links do more than provide locational information—they instead serve up content directly to the user. Page: 184

[Chunck 020312] Key words: hyperlinking; user experience; technical formalism; in-line linking; third-party server; perceptibility Essay-ready point: The server rule draws a legal distinction that ordinary users cannot perceive, because users often cannot tell whether content is hosted by the site they are viewing or pulled from a third-party server. Original Sentence: The typical viewer of a website has no way of distinguishing content which is stored on the servers of the website operator ... and content which is pulled from a third-party server through an in-line link. Page: 185

[Chunck 020313] Key words: hyperlinking; WCT; WPPT; making available; international obligations; U.S. compliance Essay-ready point: The authors argue that the server rule may place the United States at risk of under-implementing its international obligation to protect the making available right under the WCT and WPPT. Original Sentence: The server rule adopted in Perfect 10 v. Amazon may also put the United States at risk of falling short of its obligation to protect copyright owners’ ‘making available’ right under the WCT and the WPPT. Page: 191

[Chunck 020401] Key words: Article 3(1); authorisation; copyright holder; communication to the public Essay-ready point: The Court begins from the principle that Article 3(1) gives copyright holders control over each act of communication of their works to the public. Original Sentence: It follows from Article 3(1) of Directive 2001/29 that every act of communication of a work to the public has to be authorised by the copyright holder. Paragraph: 15

[Chunck 020402] Key words: communication to the public; two-part test; cumulative criteria; act of communication; public Essay-ready point: The Court held that “communication to the public” contains two cumulative requirements: first, there must be an act of communication; second, that communication must be directed to a public. Original Sentence: The concept of communication to the public includes two cumulative criteria, namely, an ‘act of communication’ of a work and the communication of that work to a ‘public’. Paragraph: 16

[Chunck 020403] Key words: communication to the public; broad interpretation; high protection; copyright holders; act of communication Essay-ready point: The Court adopted a broad interpretation of “act of communication” in order to maintain a high level of protection for copyright holders. Original Sentence: The existence of an ‘act of communication’ ... must be construed broadly ... in order to ensure ... a high level of protection for copyright holders. Paragraph: 17

[Chunck 020404] Key words: communication to the public; clickable links; direct access; protected works; hyperlinking Essay-ready point: The Court viewed clickable links as more than mere references, because they give users of the linking website direct access to protected works located on another website. Original Sentence: The provision, on a website, of clickable links to protected works published without any access restrictions on another site, affords users of the first site direct access to those works. Paragraph: 18

[Chunck 020405] Key words: communication to the public; potential access; making available; no actual use; communication Essay-ready point: For the Court, it is enough that the public is given the possibility of access; a communication may exist even if users do not actually click the link. Original Sentence: It is sufficient ... that a work is made available to a public in such a way that the persons forming that public may access it, irrespective of whether they avail themselves of that opportunity. Paragraph: 19

[Chunck 020406] Key words: communication to the public; making available; clickable links; act of communication; Article 3(1) Essay-ready point: The Court expressly held that providing clickable links to protected works is a form of “making available” and therefore an act of communication. Original Sentence: The provision of clickable links to protected works must be considered to be ‘making available’ and, therefore, an ‘act of communication’. Paragraph: 20

[Chunck 020407] Key words: communication to the public; public; indeterminate recipients; fairly large number; potential audience Essay-ready point: The Court held that “public” means an indeterminate number of potential recipients and must involve a fairly large number of persons. Original Sentence: By the term ‘public’, that provision refers to an indeterminate number of potential recipients and implies, moreover, a fairly large number of persons. Paragraph: 21

[Chunck 020408] Key words: communication to the public; website users; public element; potential users; hyperlinking Essay-ready point: The Court reasoned that links placed on a website are aimed at all potential users of that website, which satisfies the “public” element. Original Sentence: An act of communication such as that made by the manager of a website by means of clickable links is aimed at all potential users of the site ... an indeterminate and fairly large number of recipients. Paragraph: 22

[Chunck 020409] Key words: communication to the public; website manager; communication to a public; hyperlink provider; Article 3 Essay-ready point: The Court concluded that the manager of a website providing clickable links is, in principle, making a communication to a public. Original Sentence: In those circumstances, it must be held that the manager is making a communication to a public. Paragraph: 23

[Chunck 020410] Key words: communication to the public; new public; same technical means; internet communication; limitation Essay-ready point: The Court held that, where the same works are communicated on the internet by the same technical means, liability requires communication to a “new public.” Original Sentence: A communication ... concerning the same works ... made ... on the Internet, and therefore by the same technical means, must also be directed at a new public. Paragraph: 24

[Chunck 020411] Key words: communication to the public; new public; initial authorisation; copyright holder; intended audience Essay-ready point: For the Court, a “new public” means a public that the copyright holder did not take into account when authorising the initial online communication. Original Sentence: A new public, that is to say, at a public that was not taken into account by the copyright holders when they authorised the initial communication to the public. Paragraph: 24

[Chunck 020412] Key words: communication to the public; freely accessible; no new public; all internet users; authorisation Essay-ready point: The Court held that links to freely accessible works do not reach a new public, because the copyright holders had already made the works available to all internet users. Original Sentence: Making available the works concerned by means of a clickable link ... does not lead to the works in question being communicated to a new public. Paragraph: 25

[Chunck 020413] Key words: communication to the public; all internet users; initial public; free access; no restrictions Essay-ready point: Because the original newspaper site imposed no access restrictions, the Court treated all internet users as part of the public already contemplated by the copyright holders. Original Sentence: The public targeted by the initial communication consisted of all potential visitors to the site concerned ... all Internet users could therefore have free access to them. Paragraph: 26

[Chunck 020414] Key words: communication to the public; no authorisation; no new public; hyperlinking; communication to the public Essay-ready point: The Court’s decisive holding was that, although hyperlinking may be an act of communication, copyright-holder authorisation is not required if the link does not reach a new public. Original Sentence: Since there is no new public, the authorisation of the copyright holders is not required for a communication to the public such as that in the main proceedings. Paragraph: 28

[Chunck 020415] Key words: communication to the public; circumvention; access restrictions; new public; authorisation; subscribers Essay-ready point: The Court distinguished ordinary links from links that bypass access restrictions: a link that circumvents restrictions reaches a new public and therefore requires authorisation. Original Sentence: Where a clickable link makes it possible for users ... to circumvent restrictions ... all those users must be deemed to be a new public ... and accordingly the holders’ authorisation is required. Paragraph: 31

[Chunck 020501] Key words: communication to the public; preventive right; authorisation; Article 3(1); copyright control; public communication Essay-ready point: The Court viewed Article 3(1) as giving authors a preventive power to control potential communications of their works before users make those works available to the public. Original Sentence: Authors thus have a right which is preventive in nature and allows them to intervene, between possible users of their work and the communication to the public which such users might contemplate making, in order to prohibit such use. Paragraph: 28

[Chunck 020502] Key words: communication to the public; interpretation; Directive objectives; legal context; Article 3(1); scope Essay-ready point: Because Article 3(1) does not define “communication to the public,” the Court held that its meaning must be interpreted by reference to the Directive’s objectives and legal context. Original Sentence: As Article 3(1) of Directive 2001/29 does not define the concept of ‘communication to the public’, its meaning and its scope must be determined in light of the objectives pursued by that directive and of the context in which the provision being interpreted is set. Paragraph: 29

[Chunck 020503] Key words: communication to the public; high protection; appropriate reward; broad interpretation; authors; Article 3 Essay-ready point: The Court reasoned that communication to the public must be interpreted broadly because the Directive seeks a high level of protection and appropriate reward for authors. Original Sentence: The latter’s objective is to establish a high level of protection of authors, allowing them to obtain an appropriate reward for the use of their works ... ‘communication to the public’ must be interpreted broadly. Paragraph: 30

[Chunck 020504] Key words: communication to the public; fair balance; freedom of expression; information; copyright; Charter rights Essay-ready point: The Court did not treat copyright protection as absolute; it held that interpretation must preserve a fair balance between copyright holders’ property rights and users’ freedom of expression and information. Original Sentence: The harmonisation effected by it is to maintain… a fair balance between… the interests of copyright holders ... and ... the protection of the interests and fundamental rights of users ... in particular their freedom of expression and of information. Paragraph: 31

[Chunck 020505] Key words: communication to the public; two criteria; act of communication; public; cumulative test; CJEU Essay-ready point: The Court reaffirmed that communication to the public requires both an act of communication and communication of that work to a public. Original Sentence: The concept of ‘communication to the public’ includes two cumulative criteria, namely, an ‘act of communication’ of a work and the communication of that work to a ‘public’. Paragraph: 32

[Chunck 020506] Key words: communication to the public; individual assessment; case-by-case analysis; flexible criteria; communication to the public Essay-ready point: The Court held that whether there is communication to the public must be assessed individually, rather than by applying a rigid automatic rule. Original Sentence: The Court has, moreover, specified that the concept of ‘communication to the public’ requires an individual assessment. Paragraph: 33

[Chunck 020507] Key words: communication to the public; interdependent criteria; complementary factors; contextual analysis; CJEU method Essay-ready point: The Court stated that the relevant factors are complementary and interdependent, meaning they must be evaluated both separately and in combination. Original Sentence: Account has to be taken of several complementary criteria, which are not autonomous and are interdependent ... they must be applied both individually and in their interaction with one another. Paragraph: 34

[Chunck 020508] Key words: communication to the public; deliberate intervention; knowledge; indispensable role; access; protected work Essay-ready point: The Court considered the user’s indispensable role and deliberate intervention important, especially where the user acts with full knowledge to give others access to protected works. Original Sentence: The Court emphasised ... the indispensable role played by the user and the deliberate nature of its intervention. The user makes an act of communication when it intervenes, in full knowledge of the consequences of its action, to give access to a protected work. Paragraph: 35

[Chunck 020509] Key words: communication to the public; public; indeterminate viewers; large audience; potential recipients Essay-ready point: The Court confirmed that “public” means an indeterminate number of potential viewers and also requires a fairly large number of people. Original Sentence: The concept of the ‘public’ refers to an indeterminate number of potential viewers and implies, moreover, a fairly large number of people. Paragraph: 36

[Chunck 020510] Key words: communication to the public; new public; technical means; rightholder consent; Svensson; BestWater Essay-ready point: The Court held that a protected work is communicated to the public where it is transmitted by different technical means or, failing that, to a new public not previously considered by the rightholder. Original Sentence: A protected work must be communicated using specific technical means, different from those previously used or, failing that, to a ‘new public’, that is to say, to a public that was not already taken into account by the copyright holders. Paragraph: 37

[Chunck 020511] Key words: communication to the public; profit-making; commercial use; hyperlinking; relevant factor; Article 3(1) Essay-ready point: The Court treated the profit-making nature of a communication as a relevant factor in assessing whether hyperlinking amounts to communication to the public. Original Sentence: The Court has held that it is relevant that a ‘communication’, within the meaning of Article 3(1) of Directive 2001/29, is of a profit-making nature. Paragraph: 38

[Chunck 020512] Key words: communication to the public; Svensson; BestWater; consent; freely available works; hyperlinking Essay-ready point: The Court clarified that Svensson and BestWater only excluded liability where the linked works had been made freely available online with the rightholder’s consent. Original Sentence: The Court intended to refer only to the posting of hyperlinks to works which have been made freely available on another website with the consent of the rightholder. Paragraph: 41

[Chunck 020513] Key words: communication to the public; consent; authorisation; unauthorised works; Article 3(1); hyperlink liability Essay-ready point: The Court held that links to unauthorised online works cannot automatically be excluded from communication to the public, because Article 3(1) requires every act of communication to be authorised by the copyright holder. Original Sentence: Those decisions confirm the importance of such consent under that provision, as the latter specifically provides that every act of communication of a work to the public is to be authorised by the copyright holder. Paragraph: 43

[Chunck 020514] Key words: communication to the public; non-commercial linker; lack of knowledge; innocent hyperlinking; freedom of information Essay-ready point: The Court held that a non-commercial person who does not know and cannot reasonably know that the linked work was uploaded unlawfully will generally not be treated as communicating the work to the public. Original Sentence: When the posting of a hyperlink ... is carried out by a person who… does not pursue a profit, [it is necessary] to take account of the fact that that person does not know and cannot reasonably know, that that work had been published ... without the consent of the copyright holder. Paragraph: 47

[Chunck 020515] Key words: communication to the public; profit-making links; rebuttable presumption; knowledge; legality checks; GS Media Essay-ready point: The Court’s key holding is that where hyperlinks are posted for profit, the linker is expected to check legality; knowledge of the protected nature and possible lack of consent is presumed unless rebutted. Original Sentence: When the posting of hyperlinks is carried out for profit, it can be expected that the person who posted such a link carries out the necessary checks ... so that it must be presumed that that posting has occurred with the full knowledge of the protected nature of that work and the possible lack of consent. Paragraph: 51

[Chunck 020601] Key words: communication to the public; exclusive right; authorisation; making available; Article 3(1); authors Essay-ready point: The Court began from the principle that Article 3(1) gives authors the exclusive right to authorise or prohibit communication and making available of their works to the public. Original Sentence: Member States are to provide authors with the exclusive right to authorise or prohibit any communication to the public of their works ... including the making available to the public of their works ... Paragraph: 24

[Chunck 020602] Key words: communication to the public; preventive right; author control; prohibition; contemplated communication; copyright enforcement Essay-ready point: For the Court, the communication-to-the-public right is preventive because it allows authors to stop contemplated public communications before they occur. Original Sentence: Authors thus have a right which is preventive in nature and allows them to intervene between possible users of their work and the communication to the public which such users might contemplate making, in order to prohibit such communication. Paragraph: 25

[Chunck 020603] Key words: communication to the public; interpretation; Directive objectives; legal context; scope; Article 3(1) Essay-ready point: Because the Directive does not define “communication to the public,” the Court held that its scope must be determined in light of the Directive’s objectives and interpretive context. Original Sentence: As Article 3(1) of Directive 2001/29 does not define the concept of ‘communication to the public’, its meaning and its scope must be determined in light of the objectives pursued by that directive and the context in which the provision being interpreted is set. Paragraph: 26

[Chunck 020604] Key words: communication to the public; broad interpretation; high protection; appropriate reward; author remuneration; InfoSoc Directive Essay-ready point: The Court held that “communication to the public” must be interpreted broadly because the Directive aims to provide authors with high protection and appropriate remuneration. Original Sentence: The latter’s objective is to establish a high level of protection for authors, allowing them to obtain an appropriate reward for the use of their works ... ‘communication to the public’ must be interpreted broadly. Paragraph: 27

[Chunck 020605] Key words: communication to the public; individual assessment; case-specific analysis; communication to the public; CJEU approach Essay-ready point: The Court emphasised that whether conduct amounts to communication to the public must be assessed individually, according to the specific facts of the case. Original Sentence: The Court has also specified that the concept of ‘communication to the public’ ... requires an individual assessment. Paragraph: 28

[Chunck 020606] Key words: communication to the public; two-stage test; act of communication; public; cumulative criteria; Article 3 Essay-ready point: The Court applied its standard two-stage test: there must be an act of communication, and that act must be directed to a public. Original Sentence: The concept of ‘communication to the public’ includes two cumulative criteria, namely an ‘act of communication’ of a work and the communication of that work to a ‘public’ Paragraph: 29

[Chunck 020607] Key words: communication to the public; interdependent criteria; contextual analysis; complementary factors; flexible test; CJEU reasoning Essay-ready point: The Court stated that communication-to-the-public analysis is not mechanical; the relevant factors are interdependent and must be evaluated both individually and together. Original Sentence: It is necessary to take into account several complementary criteria, which are not autonomous and are interdependent ... applied both individually and in their interaction with one another. Paragraph: 30

[Chunck 020608] Key words: communication to the public; essential role; full knowledge; deliberate intervention; customer access; protected work Essay-ready point: The Court held that an act of communication may exist where a user plays an essential role and knowingly intervenes to give customers access to protected works. Original Sentence: The Court has emphasised, above all, the essential role played by the user. The user makes an act of communication when he intervenes, in full knowledge of the consequences of his action, to give access to a protected work to his customers ... Paragraph: 31

[Chunck 020609] Key words: communication to the public; public; indeterminate viewers; large number; potential recipients; audience Essay-ready point: The Court confirmed that the public element requires an indeterminate number of potential viewers and a fairly large number of people. Original Sentence: The concept of the ‘public’ refers to an indeterminate number of potential viewers and implies, moreover, a fairly large number of people. Paragraph: 32

[Chunck 020610] Key words: communication to the public; new public; technical means; rightholder consent; communication test; Article 3(1) Essay-ready point: The Court held that a work is communicated to the public if it is communicated through different technical means or, where the same means are used, to a new public not considered by the rightholder. Original Sentence: To be categorised as a ‘communication to the public’, a protected work must be communicated using specific technical means, different from those previously used or, failing that, to a ‘new public’ ... Paragraph: 33

[Chunck 020611] Key words: communication to the public; profit-making; commercial purpose; communication; Article 3(1); relevance Essay-ready point: The Court again treated the profit-making nature of the communication as relevant to the Article 3(1) assessment. Original Sentence: The Court has underlined, on many occasions, that the profit-making nature of a communication ... is not irrelevant. Paragraph: 34

[Chunck 020612] Key words: communication to the public; mere facilities; pre-installed add-ons; full knowledge; unauthorised streaming; direct access Essay-ready point: The Court distinguished the Filmspeler device from the mere provision of physical facilities because Wullems deliberately pre-installed add-ons that enabled direct access to unauthorised streaming sites. Original Sentence: The present case does not concern a situation of the ‘mere’ provision of physical facilities ... Mr Wullems, with full knowledge of the consequences of his conduct, pre-installs onto the ‘filmspeler’ multimedia player… add-ons that specifically enable purchasers to have access to protected works published — without the consent of the copyright holders ... Paragraph: 41

[Chunck 020613] Key words: communication to the public; structured menus; direct access; multimedia player; act of communication; unauthorised works Essay-ready point: The Court held that providing a player with structured-menu links to unauthorised works enabled direct access and therefore constituted an act of communication. Original Sentence: The provision of a multimedia player ... enables ... access via structured menus to links ... which, when activated by the remote control… offer its users direct access to protected works without the consent of the copyright holders and must be regarded as an act of communication ... Paragraph: 42

[Chunck 020614] Key words: communication to the public; final holding; Filmspeler; communication to the public; pre-installed links; unauthorised content Essay-ready point: The Court’s final holding was that selling a multimedia player pre-loaded with add-ons linking to freely accessible unauthorised streaming sites falls within “communication to the public” under Article 3(1). Original Sentence: The concept of ‘communication to the public’ ... must be interpreted as covering the sale of a multimedia player ... on which there are pre-installed add-ons ... containing hyperlinks to websites ... on which copyright-protected works have been made available without the consent of the right holders. Paragraph: 53

[Chunck 020701] Key words: exclusive right; authorisation; making available; Article 3(1); authors Essay-ready point: The Court began from the premise that Article 3(1) grants authors the exclusive right to authorise or prohibit any communication or making available of their works to the public. Original Sentence: Member States are required to ensure that authors have the exclusive right to authorise or prohibit any communication to the public of their works ... including the making available to the public of their works ... Paragraph: 19

[Chunck 020702] Key words: communication to the public; preventive right; author control; prohibition; contemplated communication; copyright protection Essay-ready point: The Court viewed the communication-to-the-public right as preventive because it enables authors to stop contemplated public communications of their works. Original Sentence: Authors thus have a right which is preventive in nature and allows them to intervene between possible users of their work and the communication to the public which such users might contemplate making, in order to prohibit such communication. Paragraph: 20

[Chunck 020703] Key words: communication to the public; Essay-ready point: Because Article 3(1) does not define “communication to the public,” the Court held that its meaning must be determined in light of the Directive’s objectives and interpretive context. Original Sentence: The meaning and scope of that concept must be determined in light of the objectives pursued by that directive and the context in which the provision being interpreted is set. Paragraph: 21

[Chunck 020704] Key words: communication to the public; broad interpretation; high protection; appropriate reward; authors; InfoSoc Directive Essay-ready point: The Court repeated that “communication to the public” must be interpreted broadly because the Directive aims to ensure a high level of protection and appropriate reward for authors. Original Sentence: The latter’s principal objective is to establish a high level of protection for authors, allowing them to obtain an appropriate reward for the use of their works ... the concept of ‘communication to the public’ must be interpreted broadly. Paragraph: 22

[Chunck 020705] Key words: individual assessment; fact-sensitive analysis; CJEU method; communication to the public Essay-ready point: The Court held that communication-to-the-public analysis requires an individual, fact-sensitive assessment rather than a purely formal or automatic rule. Original Sentence: The Court has also specified that the concept of ‘communication to the public’ ... requires an individual assessment. Paragraph: 23

[Chunck 020706] Key words: communication to the public; two criteria; act of communication; public; cumulative test; Article 3 Essay-ready point: The Court applied the standard two-part framework: there must be an act of communication, and that act must be directed to a public. Original Sentence: The concept of ‘communication to the public’ involves two cumulative criteria, namely an ‘act of communication’ of a work and the communication of that work to a ‘public’. Paragraph: 24

[Chunck 020707] Key words: communication to the public; interdependent criteria; complementary factors; contextual reasoning; flexible test; CJEU Essay-ready point: The Court stressed that the relevant factors are not autonomous but interdependent, so they must be assessed both individually and together. Original Sentence: It is necessary to take into account several complementary criteria, which are not autonomous and are interdependent ... applied both individually and in their interaction with one another ... Paragraph: 25

[Chunck 020708] Key words: communication to the public; deliberate intervention; full knowledge; access; protected works; essential role Essay-ready point: For the Court, a user performs an act of communication where he deliberately intervenes, with knowledge of the consequences, to give customers access to protected works that would otherwise be unavailable or difficult to access. Original Sentence: That user makes an act of communication when he intervenes, in full knowledge of the consequences of his action, to give his customers access to a protected work, particularly where, in the absence of that intervention, those customers would not be able to enjoy the broadcast work, or would be able to do so only with difficulty. Paragraph: 26

[Chunck 020709] Key words: communication to the public; public; indeterminate viewers; large audience; potential recipients; de minimis Essay-ready point: The Court reaffirmed that “public” refers to an indeterminate number of potential viewers and requires a fairly large number of persons. Original Sentence: The concept of the ‘public’ refers to an indeterminate number of potential viewers and implies, moreover, a fairly large number of people. Paragraph: 27

[Chunck 020710] Key words: communication to the public; new public; technical means; rightholder consent; communication test; Article 3 Essay-ready point: The Court stated that a protected work is communicated to the public when it is communicated through a different technical means or, if the same means are used, to a new public not contemplated by the copyright holders. Original Sentence: A protected work must be communicated using specific technical means, different from those previously used or, failing that, to a ‘new public’, that is to say, to a public that was not already taken into account by the copyright holders ... Paragraph: 28

[Chunck 020711] Key words: communication to the public; profit-making; commercial purpose; advertising revenue; Article 3(1); relevance Essay-ready point: The Court repeated that the commercial or profit-making nature of a communication is a relevant factor in assessing communication to the public. Original Sentence: The Court has underlined, on numerous occasions, that the profit-making nature of a communication ... is not irrelevant. Paragraph: 29

[Chunck 020712] Key words: communication to the public; essential role; platform operators; access; protected works; peer-to-peer Essay-ready point: Although users uploaded the files, the Court held that TPB’s operators played an essential role by making and managing a platform that enabled users to locate and share protected works. Original Sentence: Those operators, by making available and managing an online sharing platform ... intervene, with full knowledge of the consequences of their conduct, to provide access to protected works ... without the aforementioned operators making such a platform available and managing it, the works could not be shared by the users or ... sharing them on the internet would prove to be more complex. Paragraph: 36

[Chunck 020713] Key words: communication to the public; mere facilities; torrent index; search engine; active management; content filtering Essay-ready point: The Court refused to treat TPB as merely providing technical facilities, because the platform indexed torrent files, offered a search engine, categorised works, checked categories, deleted faulty files, and filtered some content. Original Sentence: The operators of the online sharing platform TPB cannot be considered to be making a ‘mere provision’ of physical facilities ... that platform indexes torrent files ... offers an index classifying the works… with the platform’s operators checking ... delete obsolete or faulty torrent files and actively filter some content. Paragraph: 38

[Chunck 020714] Key words: final holding; The Pirate Bay; communication to the public; metadata indexation; peer-to-peer Essay-ready point: The Court’s final holding was that making available and managing a sharing platform like TPB, which indexes metadata and provides a search engine enabling peer-to-peer sharing of protected works, constitutes communication to the public. Original Sentence: The concept of ‘communication to the public’ ... must be interpreted as covering ... the making available and management, on the internet, of a sharing platform which, by means of indexation of metadata relating to protected works and the provision of a search engine, allows users ... to locate those works and to share them ... Paragraph: 48

docs.title: 2.3 Seminar 3
docs.text:
[Chunck 030201] Key words: right to repair; embedded software; consumer ownership; repair control; smart devices; product functionality Essay-ready point: Modern consumer products increasingly depend on embedded software, which allows manufacturers to control repair even after the consumer has bought the physical product. Original Sentence: Cars, televisions, coffee makers, refrigerators, and printer ink cartridges are all embedded with computers and software. Without that software, these products would not function. Page: 165

[Chunck 030202] Key words: right to repair; artificial barriers; manufacturer control; repair restrictions; consumer autonomy; product design Essay-ready point: The author argues that modern repair barriers are not merely caused by technical complexity, but by manufacturers’ deliberate efforts to stop consumers from repairing their own devices. Original Sentence: This difficulty does not arise from any inherent complexities within the product itself, but rather because the manufacturers of these products do not want you tinkering with ‘their’ products. Page: 165–166

[Chunck 030203] Key words: right to repair; DRM; repair lockout; technological protection; consumer repair; access control Essay-ready point: Digital rights management can function as a repair-control mechanism, preventing consumers from carrying out basic repairs on products they have purchased. Original Sentence: Manufacturers implement digital rights management (DRM) software to artificially ‘lock out’ consumers from performing basic repairs. Page: 166

[Chunck 030204] Key words: right to repair; software licensing; ownership; hardware; repair roadblocks; EULA Essay-ready point: Manufacturers often separate hardware ownership from software control, claiming that consumers own the device but merely license the software needed to operate and repair it. Original Sentence: Manufacturers maintain that consumers own the hardware, but the manufacturers really own the software. Since consumers are only licensed to use the software, this creates an additional roadblock in any attempts to repair defective products. Page: 166

[Chunck 030205] Key words: right to repair; ownership; repair rights; consumer autonomy; third-party repair; lawful purchase Essay-ready point: The right to repair movement is grounded in the idea that lawful purchasers should be able to repair the products they own, either themselves or through third-party repairers. Original Sentence: The idea behind the right to repair is simple. You bought the device, you own it, and you should have the right to repair it. Page: 167

[Chunck 030206] Key words: right to repair; consumer safety; cybersecurity; intellectual property; manufacturer opposition; repair legislation Essay-ready point: Manufacturers justify opposition to right-to-repair legislation by invoking consumer safety, cybersecurity, and intellectual property protection. Original Sentence: Manufacturers who oppose the right to repair claim they are promoting consumer safety, reducing cybersecurity risks, and protecting their intellectual property portfolio. Page: 167

[Chunck 030207] Key words: right to repair; anti-competitive practices; e-waste; inefficiency; property rights; repair monopoly Essay-ready point: Supporters argue that manufacturer-controlled repair is anti-competitive, inefficient, harmful to consumer property rights, and contributes to electronic waste. Original Sentence: Proponents of the right to repair argue that manufacturers’ practices are anti-competitive, inefficient, contribute to an increasing amount of e-waste, and infringe on consumer property rights. Page: 167

[Chunck 030208] Key words: right to repair; Massachusetts law; repair manuals; replacement parts; automotive repair; legislative model Essay-ready point: The Massachusetts automotive right-to-repair law demonstrates that legislation can require manufacturers to provide repair manuals and parts to the public. Original Sentence: The bill requires car manufacturers to provide manuals and replacement parts to the public for the purpose of repair. Page: 167

[Chunck 030209] Key words: right to repair; DMCA; anti-circumvention; DRM; embedded software; repair barriers Essay-ready point: The DMCA can obstruct repair because it prohibits circumvention of technological measures that control access to copyrighted software embedded in devices. Original Sentence: The DMCA makes it illegal to circumvent a technological measure (e.g., DRM) that effectively controls access to copyrighted works. Page: 168

[Chunck 030210] Key words: right to repair; DMCA exemptions; narrow scope; repair tools; manuals; software-embedded devices Essay-ready point: Although the 2018 DMCA exemptions recognised some repair rights for software-embedded devices, the author criticises them as narrow because they apply only to limited categories and do not provide access to tools, manuals, or parts. Original Sentence: These exemptions are extremely narrow and only apply to specific categories including smartphones, home appliances, Internet of Things gadgets, and motorized land vehicles. Further, they do not provide repairers access to manuals, parts, or software tools ... Page: 168

[Chunck 030211] Key words: right to repair; EULA; terms of service; resale; repair restriction; ownership Essay-ready point: Beyond copyright law, manufacturers use EULAs and terms of service to frame consumers as licensees rather than owners, further restricting repair and resale. Original Sentence: Corporations rely on Terms of Service (TOS) agreements and End User License Agreements (EULAs) to further restrict consumers’ ability to repair and resell their own products. Page: 168

[Chunck 030212] Key words: right to repair; John Deere; repair monopoly; diagnostics software; TPM; farming equipment Essay-ready point: John Deere’s tractors show how DRM, proprietary diagnostics, and embedded software can turn repair into a manufacturer-controlled monopoly, especially harming farmers who need fast repairs. Original Sentence: The computer systems embedded in the equipment utilize DRM and Technological Protection Measures (TPM) to reject non-proprietary parts. Further, repairers need access to John Deere’s diagnostics software to repair the equipment. Page: 169

[Chunck 030213] Key words: right to repair; authorised repair; revenue stream; diagnostics; repair monopoly; proprietary tools Essay-ready point: By restricting access to diagnostic software and proprietary tools, manufacturers can compel consumers to use authorised repair networks, creating an additional revenue stream. Original Sentence: By adding these hurdles to repair, John Deere maintains an additional revenue stream because they force farmers to utilize their authorized repair network to repair equipment. Page: 169–170

[Chunck 030214] Key words: right to repair; intellectual property; innovation; economic development; repair rights; competition Essay-ready point: The author argues that intellectual property law should encourage creativity and innovation, not be used to prevent repair, restrain competition, or block economic development. Original Sentence: Intellectual property laws were created to protect creativity and promote innovation, not to stifle economic development. Page: 169

[Chunck 030215] Key words: right to repair; model legislation; repair tools; spare parts; manuals; DRM bypass information Essay-ready point: A meaningful right to repair requires more than a legal permission to repair; it also requires practical access to documents, parts, tools, and information needed to bypass technological restrictions. Original Sentence: The model legislation seeks to make available documents, parts, tools, and information to bypass DRM measures to facilitate repair. Page: 183

[Chunck 030301] Key words: right to repair; repair cost; replacement; consumer choice; Apple; economic incentives Essay-ready point: Right-to-repair concerns arise because manufacturers can make repair economically unattractive, encouraging consumers to replace functioning devices rather than repair them. Original Sentence: Apple currently charges $279 for this fairly straightforward repair, a fee that often makes purchasing a new phone more attractive. Page: 361–362

[Chunck 030302] Key words: right to repair; profit incentive; replacement; manufacturer strategy; repair market; consumer welfare Essay-ready point: Manufacturers may prefer replacement because new product sales generate far higher profits than repair services, creating a structural conflict between corporate incentives and consumer repair interests. Original Sentence: Apple’s apparent preference for replacement over repair is economically rational. Page: 362

[Chunck 030303] Key words: right to repair; repair restrictions; farmers; hospitals; cars; medical devices Essay-ready point: The right-to-repair problem extends beyond smartphones: car owners, farmers, photographers, and hospitals also face restrictions that limit their ability to repair essential devices and equipment. Original Sentence: Car owners, farmers, photographers, and even hospitals are forced to contend with repair restrictions. Page: 362–363

[Chunck 030304] Key words: right to repair; economic restrictions; technological barriers; legal threats; repair control; IP claims Essay-ready point: Repair restrictions are not caused by one single mechanism; manufacturers combine economic pricing, product design, software control, warranty threats, and intellectual-property claims to discourage independent repair. Original Sentence: Device makers rely on an assortment of economic, technological, and legal techniques to curtail repair. Page: 363

[Chunck 030305] Key words: right to repair; embedded software; cloud software; post-sale control; smart products; repair restriction Essay-ready point: As devices increasingly depend on embedded or cloud-based software, manufacturers gain greater practical power to limit repairs even after consumers have purchased the physical product. Original Sentence: As products increasingly depend on local or cloud-based software code for their basic functionality, device makers have even greater power to restrict repair. Page: 363

[Chunck 030306] Key words: right to repair; e-waste; sustainability; toxic waste; replacement culture; environmental harm Essay-ready point: The right to repair is also an environmental issue because replacing rather than repairing devices contributes to massive electronic waste and toxic pollution. Original Sentence: About 1.5 billion mobile phones are sold annually worldwide, contributing to the more than fifty million tons of electronic waste produced every year. Page: 363

[Chunck 030307] Key words: right to repair; software update; third-party repair; bricked devices; Apple; repair deterrence Essay-ready point: Manufacturers can use software updates to punish or prevent independent repair, as illustrated by devices that were disabled after Apple software detected third-party repair. Original Sentence: Phones that were working normally for weeks or months were suddenly ‘bricked’ after the installation of an Apple software update. Page: 367

[Chunck 030308] Key words: right to repair; planned obsolescence; software throttling; replacement; product lifespan; consumer deception Essay-ready point: Modern planned obsolescence is not limited to physical design; software can artificially reduce performance and push consumers toward buying replacement products. Original Sentence: Today, they can leverage software to artificially degrade product performance and spur consumers to buy replacements. Page: 367

[Chunck 030309] Key words: right to repair; cloud dependence; remote servers; smart products; repair access; digital obsolescence Essay-ready point: When product functionality depends on remote servers rather than local hardware, owners may be unable to repair or preserve the product once the manufacturer withdraws support. Original Sentence: Although Jibo’s physical components could be repaired, most of its features were housed on a remote server that Jibo owners could not access, let alone repair. Page: 368

[Chunck 030310] Key words: right to repair; high repair prices; economic barrier; replacement incentive; consumer decision-making; repair market Essay-ready point: Manufacturers can discourage repair by charging prices high enough to narrow the difference between repair and replacement, making a new device appear more rational. Original Sentence: One way to narrow that gap is by charging high prices for repair. Page: 368

[Chunck 030311] Key words: right to repair; replacement parts; diagnostics; manuals; schematics; independent repair Essay-ready point: A central obstacle to repair is manufacturers’ control over the practical inputs needed for repair, including parts, diagnostic tools, schematics, and manuals. Original Sentence: Firms make it difficult to acquire replacement parts ... control access to diagnostic tools ... And they lock down schematics and manuals that would facilitate repair. Page: 369

[Chunck 030312] Key words: right to repair; John Deere; software authentication; replacement parts; farmers; repair monopoly Essay-ready point: Software authentication systems can prevent owners and independent repair shops from replacing even simple parts unless the manufacturer authorises the repair. Original Sentence: The software embedded in John Deere tractors ... requires authentication of new parts before the vehicle will recognize them. Page: 370

[Chunck 030313] Key words: right to repair; DMCA; § 1201; digital locks; anti-circumvention; repair liability Essay-ready point: Original Sentence: These digital locks pose practical hurdles for repair. But § 1201 compounds those difficulties by introducing potential legal liability for repairers who remove or bypass such digital locks. Page: 371

[Chunck 030314] Key words: right to repair; DMCA exemptions; circumvention tools; temporary exemptions; repair advocates; legal limits Essay-ready point: Although DMCA exemptions are important for repair advocates, they remain limited because they exclude many devices, are temporary, and do not permit sharing circumvention tools. Original Sentence: These exemptions, while an important success for repair advocates, are limited in important respects ... while it is lawful to circumvent in order to repair these devices, it remains unlawful to create or share tools that enable circumvention. Page: 371

[Chunck 030315] Key words: right to repair; consumer expectations; survey evidence; independent repair; legal intervention; repair freedom Essay-ready point: Survey evidence supports legal intervention because consumers overwhelmingly believe they should be able to repair devices themselves or choose an independent repair shop. Original Sentence: More than 80% of respondents expressed their belief that they have the right to repair devices themselves or to rely on the repair shop of their choice. Page: 392

[Chunck 030401] Key words: right to repair; IoT repair; hardware; software; data; socio-technical ecosystem Essay-ready point: The right to repair is especially complex for IoT devices because repair is not limited to replacing hardware; it also involves software, data, cybersecurity, manufacturers, retailers, users, and designers. Original Sentence: IoT systems pose unique challenges for repair as they implicate hardware, software, and data jointly in a complex ecosystem of actors such as users, designers, manufacturers, and retailers. Page: 1

[Chunck 030402] Key words: right to repair; post-sale control; manufacturer power; IoT devices; software restrictions; consumer relationship Essay-ready point: Unlike conventional goods, IoT products may remain subject to post-sale control because manufacturers can alter, service, or restrict functionality through software and connectivity. Original Sentence: Products can continue to be altered, serviced or restricted past the point of sale by manufacturers. The relationship between manufacturer and consumer is more intricate and ongoing than conventional products. Page: 1

[Chunck 030403] Key words: right to repair; planned obsolescence; upgrades; product lifespan; e-waste; consumer rights Essay-ready point: A central justification for right-to-repair laws is that planned obsolescence shortens product life and pushes consumers into repeated upgrades, creating both consumer-rights and environmental problems. Original Sentence: Planned obsolescence ... [is] a practice where manufacturers intentionally design products with a limited lifespan, making repairs difficult or impossible ... consumers find themselves trapped in a cycle of constant upgrades, contributing to electronic waste and environmental concerns. Page: 2

[Chunck 030404] Key words: right to repair; modularity; proprietary design; throwaway culture; faulty components; third-party repair Essay-ready point: The authors argue that proprietary and non-modular design undermines repair because a single defective part may cause the entire IoT device to be discarded. Original Sentence: Manufacturers often employ proprietary designs, making it difficult for consumers or third-party repair services to access and replace faulty components. This lack of modularity not only obstructs repairs but also contributes to a throwaway culture. Page: 2

[Chunck 030405] Key words: right to repair; embedded software; diagnostic tools; source code; independent repair; manufacturer dependence Essay-ready point: Independent repair becomes harder when software is tightly integrated with hardware because consumers and repairers need access to source code and diagnostic tools. Original Sentence: Many IoT devices have embedded software tightly intertwined with the hardware, hindering independent repair efforts. Without access to source codes and diagnostic tools, users are left at the mercy of manufacturers. Page: 2

[Chunck 030406] Key words: right to repair; software updates; device obsolescence; maintenance; product lifespan; IoT Essay-ready point: Repairability must include software maintenance because limited update support can render otherwise functional IoT devices obsolete. Original Sentence: Limited support for software updates can render devices obsolete, forcing consumers to purchase new models rather than maintaining and repairing their existing ones. Page: 2

[Chunck 030407] Key words: right to repair; consumer autonomy; privacy; choice; sustainability; repair control Essay-ready point: The right to repair is connected to broader consumer rights because restrictions on repair limit consumer autonomy and affect privacy, choice, product longevity, security, and sustainability. Original Sentence: The right to repair is challenged as manufacturers retain tight control over repair processes, limiting consumer autonomy ... ultimately impacting their rights to privacy, choice, and sustainability. Page: 2

[Chunck 030408] Key words: right to repair; cybersecurity; transparency; accountability; updates; IoT resilience Essay-ready point: The article suggests that repair access should not be framed only as a cybersecurity risk; empowering users to repair and update devices may improve IoT resilience. Original Sentence: The right to repair is intricately linked to the need for transparency and accountability in addressing cybersecurity threats, as empowering users to fix and update their devices can enhance the overall resilience of the IoT ecosystem. Page: 2

[Chunck 030409] Key words: right to repair; circular economy; sustainability; repairability; IoT technology; product lifespan Essay-ready point: Right-to-repair policy is closely linked to circular economy objectives because repair extends product lifespans, reduces waste, and promotes more sustainable relationships with technology. Original Sentence: There has been a growing call for greater repairability of IoT technology alongside wider calls to move towards more circular economies and sustainable relationships with technologies. Page: 1

[Chunck 030410] Key words: right to repair; EU policy; environmental motivation; circular economy; repair legislation; sustainability Essay-ready point: The EU’s approach to repair is largely framed through environmental policy and circularity, rather than only through individual consumer ownership. Original Sentence: Numerous jurisdictions have begun implementing policies that facilitate a future right to repair. This policy direction has largely been guided by environmental motivations, with many markets now transitioning towards a ‘circular economy’. Page: 5

[Chunck 030411] Key words: European Commission; repair of goods; EU proposal; right to repair; consumer repair Essay-ready point: The authors describe the European Commission’s 2023 proposal on promoting repair of goods as a right to repair in substance, even if not always labelled as such. Original Sentence: In March 2023, the European Commission announced a proposal promoting the repair of goods… This is essentially a right to repair in all but name. Page: 5

[Chunck 030412] Key words: right to repair; repairability index; France; disclosure; manuals; consumer choice Essay-ready point: France’s repairability index illustrates a consumer-facing regulatory model that uses product information to influence purchasing behaviour toward more repairable and sustainable goods. Original Sentence: France ... mandated the inclusion of the ‘L’indice de réparabilité’ ... [which] requires that manufacturers provide information on: a products projected lifespan, access to repair components, access to manuals and repair directions, and its waste or recyclability. Page: 6

[Chunck 030413] Key words: right to repair; repair definition; mending; customization; repurposing; tinkering Essay-ready point: A strong essay point is that right-to-repair debates should define “repair” carefully, because repair may mean mending, customising, repurposing, or tinkering with a device. Original Sentence: The literature appears to suggest four formulations ... repair as mending ... repair as ‘customization’ ... repair as ‘re-purposing’ ... ‘repair as tinkering’ Page: 8
